inputs.original_text: The conflict involving the US, Israel and Iran is pushing oil costs upward, and ordinary households and workers will feel the squeeze first—not those with the most wealth or power. Cutting excise duties may steady petrol and diesel prices for now, but it also means less public revenue, with the bill potentially shifted onto people later. This is a reminder that dependence on imported crude leaves India exposed to global shocks. We need an energy system built around resilience and fairness, rather than one that repeatedly makes people already struggling with living costs absorb the consequences.
inputs.modified_text:
The US-Israel-Iran conflict is a blunt reminder that when India depends on imported crude, turmoil abroad can hit families at home. Workers and ordinary households feel higher fuel costs first, so cutting excise duties to ease the pressure is the right instinct—even if governments must manage the loss of revenue responsibly rather than simply passing the bill along later.

The deeper answer is national resilience: a dependable energy system that protects households from foreign shocks. We should put energy security and the interests of working families ahead of fashionable promises that leave the country exposed.
